idiom_name: port interface + adapter class + record DTOs, with explicit interface implementation at the seam
implementation_notes: The layer is hand-written from ordinary C#: the domain declares an interface (IOrderPort), the adapter holds the vendor client in a private readonly field and translates each call, boundary models are records (record LegacyOrderDto(string OrderId, int Qty)) so value equality and init-only immutability come free, and System.Text.Json - including JsonConverter<T> or [JsonPropertyName] - owns only the wire half. Async upstream APIs are mapped to the domain's own task and error contract with CancellationToken threaded through. The fuller facade + adapter + translator decomposition is still justified when one adapter fronts several upstream calls or when the mapping is injected for tests; for a single call path the interface plus mapping methods is the whole pattern.
pitfalls: Vendor types leaking through the port (HttpResponseMessage, JsonElement, JsonDocument): the domain then depends on the transport library even though an interface exists.
Async-over-sync: blocking on .Result/.Wait() inside the adapter deadlocks under a SynchronizationContext and hides upstream latency from cancellation.
Record DTOs are only shallowly immutable - a mutable collection in a record component still crosses the seam by reference and can be changed by both sides.
Exception vocabulary: letting HttpRequestException/TaskCanceledException escape the adapter re-imports transport errors as domain errors.
